name: Car-following models (IDM, Krauss, Gipps, Wiedemann-74/99, Nagel-Schreckenberg) and their Indian calibrations
maintainer: Academic models: IDM by Treiber, Hennecke and Helbing (2000); Krauss by S. Krauss (1998, SUMO default); Gipps by P.G. Gipps (1981); Wiedemann-74/99 by R. Wiedemann (PTV Vissim); Nagel-Schreckenberg cellular automaton by K. Nagel and M. Schreckenberg (1992). Indian calibrations by IIT Madras / TU Dresden (Kanagaraj, Treiber, Chaudhari, Kulkarni, Asaithambi), IIT Bombay (Mathew, Ravishankar) and NIT Karnataka.
last_activity: 2026: arXiv 2608.00602 'Beyond Lanes' (Agrawal, Asaithambi, Kanagaraj, Treiber, Okhrin, Kumara; submitted 1 Aug 2026) publishes per-class desired time gap and standstill gap from Chennai UAV data; a Non-Lane-Based IDM paper appeared in Transportation Research Part C in 2026 [uncertain].
licence: Models are published equations (no licence). Reference implementations: SUMO (EPL-2.0) implements Krauss, IDM, EIDM, W99, Wiedemann; Treiber's mixedTraffic JavaScript (GPL-3.0) implements IDM/ACC-based 2D model.
language: Language-independent equations; reference implementations in C++ (SUMO) and JavaScript (Treiber's traffic-simulation.de / mixedTraffic).
code_availability: Source available: SUMO car-following models (https://sumo.dlr.de/docs/Car-Following-Models.html, https://github.com/eclipse-sumo/sumo) and Treiber's JS implementation (https://github.com/MTGermany/mixedTraffic). Indian calibration studies are paper-only; no calibration code released.
maintenance_health: IDM and Krauss are actively maintained inside SUMO. Indian IDM calibration research is active (IIT Madras + TU Dresden group published 2018, 2024, 2026). Per-class Indian parameter sets are scattered across papers and not packaged in any simulator.
scale: Microscopic (IDM, Krauss, Gipps, Wiedemann are time-continuous or time-step car-following; Nagel-Schreckenberg is a microscopic cellular automaton with 7.5 m cells and 1 s steps).
car_following: IDM equation: dv/dt = a * [1 - (v/v0)^delta - (s*(v,dv)/s)^2], with desired gap s*(v,dv) = s0 + v*T + v*dv / (2*sqrt(a*b)); v = own speed, s = bumper-to-bumper gap, dv = v - v_leader (approach rate). Parameters: v0 desired speed, T desired time gap, s0 minimum standstill gap, a maximum acceleration, b comfortable deceleration, delta = 4. Original example values (Treiber et al. 2000, Wikipedia table): v0 = 30 m/s, T = 1.5 s, s0 = 2 m, a = 0.73 m/s2, b = 1.67 m/s2, delta = 4, vehicle length 5 m. Commonly used Treiber/Kesting textbook defaults: highway v0 = 120 km/h, T = 1.0-1.5 s, s0 = 2 m, a = 1.0 m/s2, b = 1.5 m/s2; city v0 = 54 km/h [uncertain]. KRAUSS (SUMO default): v_safe = v_l + (g - v_l*tau) / ((v + v_l)/(2*b) + tau); v_des = min(v_max, v + a*dt, v_safe); v_next = max(0, random(v_des - sigma*a*dt, v_des)); SUMO defaults accel = 2.6 m/s2, decel = 4.5 m/s2, emergencyDecel = 9 m/s2, sigma = 0.5, tau = 1.0 s, minGap = 2.5 m. GIPPS: v(t+tau) = min{ v + 2.5*a*tau*(1 - v/V)*sqrt(0.025 + v/V), b*tau + sqrt(b^2*tau^2 - b*[2*(x_l - s_l - x) - v*tau - v_l^2/b_hat]) }; IIT Bombay (Ravishankar and Mathew 2011, J. Transp. Eng. 137(11)) modified Gipps to use leader-follower vehicle-type dependent parameters. WIEDEMANN-99: 10 parameters CC0-CC9; Vissim defaults CC0 = 1.5 m, CC1 = 0.9 s, CC2 = 4 m, CC3 = -8 s, CC4 = -0.35 m/s, CC5 = 0.35 m/s, CC6 = 11.44, CC7 = 0.25 m/s2, CC8 = 3.5 m/s2, CC9 = 1.5 m/s2 [uncertain for CC0/CC9; the arXiv 2405.10665 appendix lists CC0 = 0.65 m]. NAGEL-SCHRECKENBERG: per step (1) v = min(v+1, vmax), (2) v = min(v, gap), (3) with probability p v = max(v-1, 0), (4) x = x + v; standard vmax = 5 cells, cell 7.5 m, dt 1 s.
lane_model: All five models are single-file (one leader). They need an external lane-change model (MOBIL for IDM, SUMO LC2013/SL2015 for Krauss) or an extension that picks the leader by lateral overlap in non-lane traffic. Indian studies identify the leader as the nearest vehicle ahead with lateral overlap (follower and candidate widths overlapping), optionally with a lateral-clearance tolerance (arXiv 2405.10665 'lateral clear gap' method M8 performed best).
lateral_model_type: None in the base models. Extensions: Kanagaraj and Treiber (2018) generalise IDM/ACC to a 2D force field (continuous 2D lateral model); SUMO sublane model adds sublane lateral positioning for any car-following model; Gunay (2007) staggered following with lateral discomfort.
junction_model: Not part of car-following models. In SUMO, junction right-of-way and signals are handled by the junction model, with the car-following model used to compute stopping at the stop line (leader = virtual stopped vehicle). Same approach applies to any IDM implementation: treat red signal / yield point as a standing obstacle at s = distance to stop line.
signal_control_modes: Not applicable to the model itself; signals act as virtual obstacles to the car-following model.
flyover_support: Not applicable (car-following is network-agnostic; works on any link including ramps). Merges need a gap-acceptance or lane-change model on top.
vehicle_types: Parameterised per class by changing v0, T, s0, a, b and vehicle length/width. Published Indian per-class IDM sets exist for motorcycle, car, bus and auto-rickshaw (Kanagaraj and Treiber 2018). Gipps variant of Ravishankar and Mathew uses leader-follower type pairs.
gridlock_policy: Not applicable to the models. Note: Krauss and IDM are collision-free in theory; IDM with large time steps (Euler, dt > ~0.5 s) at very small s0 can produce negative gaps, so implementations should clamp gaps and use dt <= 0.2-0.5 s [uncertain].
mixed_traffic_support: Partial. Base models assume homogeneous lane-based following. Indian studies show parameters differ strongly by follower class and by leader-follower pair, and IDM, Gipps and Wiedemann can reproduce Indian following behaviour reasonably well once calibrated per class (JITS 2019 calibration of Wiedemann-74/99, Gipps, Bando OVM and IDM per follower category, DOI 10.1080/15472450.2019.1675522).
non_lane_behaviour: Base models have none. The Kanagaraj and Treiber (2018) Mixed Traffic flow Model (MTM) turns IDM into a 2D model: longitudinal acceleration from the most restrictive leader among laterally overlapping/near vehicles (attenuated by lateral distance with scale s_y0 = 0.15 m), and lateral speed from an optimal-velocity-like relaxation with desired lateral speed driven by acceleration differences among neighbours (lambda = 0.4 s, tau = 1 s, max heading 0.2 rad, politeness p = 0.2). In single-file following it reduces exactly to IDM. A 2026 Non-Lane-Based IDM was calibrated on Chennai trajectories [uncertain on details].
seepage_filtering_support: Not by itself. Filtering emerges only when combined with a lateral model (2D MTM, SUMO sublane, strip-based) plus small two-wheeler width and small s0 / T (Indian two-wheeler s0 ~ 0.5 m, T ~ 0.3-0.5 s).
per_class_parameters: 1) Kanagaraj and Treiber 2018 (Physica A 509, arXiv 1805.05076), IDM/ACC calibrated on Chennai six-lane arterial with genetic algorithm (bmax = 9 m/s2 for all): Motorcycle L 1.8 m, W 0.6 m, v0 25-18 m/s, T 0.3 s, s0 0.5 m, a 2.0 m/s2, b 2.0 m/s2; Car L 4.2 m, W 1.7 m, v0 18-12 m/s, T 0.8 s, s0 2.0 m, a 1.0, b 1.0; Bus L 10.3 m, W 2.1 m, v0 14-10 m/s, T 1.0 s, s0 2.0 m, a 1.0, b 1.0; Auto-rickshaw L 2.6 m, W 0.9 m, v0 range printed as '5-6' m/s [uncertain - likely extraction issue], T 1.0 s, s0 2.0 m, a 1.0, b 1.0. 2) Agrawal et al. 2026 (arXiv 2608.00602), Chennai Saidapet UAV data, steady-state desired time gap median (mean): two-wheeler 0.49 s (0.67), car 1.21 s (1.34), auto-rickshaw 0.81 s (0.92), LCV 1.08 s (1.25), HCV 1.57 s (1.86); standstill minimum gap median (mean): TW 0.55 m (0.73), car 1.32 m (1.46), AR 0.83 m (1.04), LCV 0.99 m (1.20), HCV 0.71 m (0.83). Use these medians directly as IDM T and s0 per class. 3) Kulkarni, Chaudhari, Srinivasan, Chilukuri, Treiber, Okhrin (arXiv 2405.10665), Wiedemann-99 for car followers in Chennai with proposed lateral-clear-gap leader identification: CC1 = 0.303 s, CC2 = 6.80 m, CC3 = -3.71 s, CC4 = -2.44 m/s, CC5 = 2.41 m/s, CC7 = 0.665 m/s2, CC8 = 3.06 m/s2 (bootstrap means). 4) SUMO Krauss per-vClass defaults (not Indian): motorcycle L 2.2 m, W 0.9 m, accel 6 m/s2, decel 10 m/s2; passenger L 5 m, W 1.8 m, accel 2.6, decel 4.5; bus L 12 m, W 2.5 m, accel 1.2, decel 4; bicycle L 1.6 m, W 0.65 m, accel 1.2, decel 3, minGap 0.5 m.
indian_calibration_evidence: Kanagaraj and Treiber 2018: MTM with IDM base calibrated on medium traffic, validated on congested traffic in Chennai; travel time, entry/exit flow within 20% of observation (calibration avg travel time 7.24 s observed vs 6.16 s simulated; validation 12.82 s vs 13.41 s); lateral-shift count off in congested case (14 observed vs 9 simulated). Kulkarni et al. (arXiv 2405.10665): W99 calibrated for 623 car-follower pairs (70/30 split for validation); leader identification method changes calibrated parameters significantly (CC1 0.30 s vs 0.56 s depending on method). JITS 2019 study calibrated Wiedemann-74/99, Gipps, Bando and IDM per follower class and found IDM, Gipps and Wiedemann resemble Indian behaviour reasonably well. Ravishankar and Mathew 2011 vehicle-type dependent Gipps assessed micro and macro on homogeneous and heterogeneous data. NITK thesis compared Gipps, IDM, Krauss and Das-Asundi across car-2W, 2W-auto, HV-2W pairs.
calibration_dataset_used: Chennai six-lane divided arterial (bridge section, 245-250 m, 11.2-12 m carriageway) video trajectories from Kanagaraj et al. 2015 (3016 vehicles, 30 min, 57% two-wheelers, 27% cars, 12% three-wheelers, 3% buses); Chennai Saidapet UAV dataset 26 June 2023 (550 m, 36 min, 0.04 s resolution, ~5,891 trajectories). Openness of both: the 2015 Chennai dataset has been shared by the authors on request [uncertain]; the 2023 UAV data availability is not stated in the arXiv page.
calibration_method: Kanagaraj and Treiber 2018: MATLAB genetic algorithm minimising root of summed squared relative errors over 5 macroscopic measures (mean travel time, its SD, entry flow, exit flow, number of lateral shifts). Kulkarni et al.: joint leader-follower identification and parameter estimation minimising RMSE of position, with bootstrapping for parameter significance. JITS 2019: per-class calibration from trajectory data [uncertain on optimiser].
max_density_tested: Kanagaraj and Treiber 2018 congested validation: 450 motorcycles/km + 225 cars/km + 35 buses/km + 80 autos/km (1D partial densities on ~12 m roadway). Agrawal et al. 2026 observed area densities up to ~0.33 veh/m2 in two-wheeler/auto dominated states.
validation_against_field_case: Chennai six-lane urban arterial (Kanagaraj et al. 2015 site) and Saidapet, Chennai (13.0209 N, 80.2254 E) UAV section. No Bengaluru (Hebbal/Silk Board) car-following calibration found.
reuse_mode: Port the model: implement IDM (about 15 lines) as the longitudinal core, parameterised per vehicle class with Indian values; use Krauss only if adopting SUMO as engine (it is SUMO's default and SUMO also ships IDM via carFollowModel="IDM").
effort_within_72_hours: IDM per-class implementation plus leader selection by lateral overlap: 2-4 hours including unit tests (free-road acceleration to v0, stopping behind standing obstacle at s0, no negative gaps). Cut: Wiedemann (10 parameters, regime logic, poorly documented defaults), Gipps (reaction-time delay buffers), formal calibration (use published Chennai values instead), stochastic noise beyond a simple speedFactor distribution. Nagel-Schreckenberg is fastest to code but its 7.5 m cell cannot represent 2 m two-wheelers, so skip it.
licence_constraint: None for equations. Copying SUMO code imposes EPL-2.0 (file-level copyleft); copying Treiber's mixedTraffic JS imposes GPL-3.0 on the combined work - reimplement from the paper instead to keep licensing free.
known_limitations: IDM: deterministic, no reaction time, gives unrealistic hard braking when a vehicle cuts in at a very small gap (Treiber's IIDM/ACC variants address this); delta and b interplay causes overshoot in very dense stop-and-go. Krauss: stochastic dawdling sigma = 0.5 makes it noisy and lowers capacity; parameters are not behaviourally interpretable for Indian classes. Gipps: requires reaction-time delay, conservative capacity. Wiedemann-99: many parameters, regime thresholds sensitive, calibration ill-posed; Indian calibrations depend strongly on how the leader is identified (CC1 changes from 0.56 s to 0.30 s by changing the identification method). Nagel-Schreckenberg: 7.5 m cells, single class, no lateral movement. All: designed for single-file following; in Indian traffic followers often have multiple partial leaders and intermittent following, so the same parameters behave differently depending on leader-selection logic. Calibrated Indian values come from a few Chennai mid-block sections, not from intersections or Bengaluru.
documented_failures: Kanagaraj and Treiber 2018: number of lateral shifts underpredicted in congested validation (9 vs 14 observed), attributed to more aggressive or cooperative behaviour not in the model. Kulkarni et al.: headway-threshold-based leader identification gave significantly different (biased) parameters; a 0.5 s change in the headway threshold notably changed the identified pairs. Agrawal et al. 2026: one-dimensional models cannot adequately describe the observed disordered traffic states.
validation_approach: Trajectory-level RMSE of position for leader-follower pairs (hold-out 30%); macroscopic validation by travel time, flows and lateral shifts on a different traffic state (calibrate on medium, validate on congested); fundamental-diagram comparison.
takeaway_for_our_build: Use IDM as the single longitudinal model for all classes, with per-class parameters taken from Indian data: two-wheeler T 0.5 s, s0 0.5 m, a 2.0 m/s2, b 2.0 m/s2; car T 1.2 s, s0 1.3-2.0 m, a 1.0-1.5 m/s2, b 1.5 m/s2; auto-rickshaw T 0.8 s, s0 0.8 m, a 1.0 m/s2; bus/HCV T 1.5 s, s0 1.0-2.0 m, a 1.0 m/s2; delta = 4, bmax 9 m/s2 clamp. Pick the leader as the nearest vehicle ahead whose lateral extent overlaps the follower's (plus a small clearance), not the vehicle in the same lane. Integrate with dt = 0.1-0.2 s using ballistic update and clamp v >= 0 and gap >= 0. Keep the parameter table as editable data in scenario JSON so users can tweak classes. Do not spend time on Wiedemann or calibration inside 72 hours; cite the Chennai sources in the UI as parameter provenance.
